title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation Contractor | Genstone
metaDescription: Renovations for duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and two-flats: shared systems, occupied-unit phasing, unit separation and scopes built around rents or resale.
h1: Small Multifamily Renovations for Two- to Four-Unit Buildings
lede: Duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes and two-flats sit between single-family and apartment buildings, and their renovations have problems neither one does. Systems are shared, units may be occupied, the legal unit count matters and the value depends on rents as much as finishes. Genstone Construction renovates small multifamily buildings for investors and owner-occupants with scopes that treat the building as one asset and each unit as its own home.

sections.h2: Why two-to-four unit buildings need their own approach
sections.body:
Small multifamily buildings are usually financed and regulated as residential property, which is a large part of their appeal. An investor can buy a fourplex with residential financing, an owner-occupant can live in one unit and rent the others, and the building can be renovated under residential codes in most jurisdictions. But the work itself is closer to a small apartment project than a house flip.

The differences show up quickly. A single roof, foundation, sewer line and often a single heating plant serve several households. The building may have separate electrical meters or a shared service. Units may be in very different condition, with one recently updated and another untouched for decades. Some units may be occupied by tenants with leases that run past closing. And the value of the building at refinance or resale is driven heavily by the rent each unit can command.

That means the scope has to work at two levels. At the building level, the questions are about the envelope, the structure, the shared systems and code items like fire separation and egress. At the unit level, the questions are about finishes, layouts, appliances and the rent or resale price each unit can support.

Genstone renovates two-to-four unit buildings for fix-and-flip investors, BRRRR investors, long-term holders and owner-occupants using FHA 203(k) financing. Our scopes separate building-wide work from unit-by-unit work, so you can see exactly what each part of the project costs and how it supports the plan for the property.

sections.h2: Know the building you are buying
sections.body:
Small multifamily stock varies a great deal by region and era, and the building type shapes what the renovation involves. Some of the common types we see:

- Two-flats and three-flats: stacked units, one per floor, common in older Midwestern cities. They often have a shared basement, a front and rear stair, and rear porches that need regular structural attention.
- Triple-deckers: three stacked units with stacked porches, common in older New England cities. Wood frame construction and stacked porches bring their own fire separation and maintenance considerations.
- Up-down duplexes: one unit above another in a house-like building, often with a shared entry or stair.
- Side-by-side duplexes: two units sharing a party wall, including the shotgun doubles found in parts of the South.
- Fourplexes: often purpose-built in the middle decades of the last century, with a central stair or individual entries.
- Converted single-family homes: large older houses divided into units at some point, sometimes with permits and sometimes without.

That last category deserves caution. Before you underwrite a building on its unit count, confirm that the units are legal. Basement or attic units added without permits are common, and a unit the city does not recognize may need to be brought into compliance, removed or simply left out of the rent roll. Zoning, egress, ceiling height and fire separation requirements all come into play.

During a Pre-Offer Rehab Review, we look at how the building is configured, which systems are shared, and whether anything about the unit layout suggests a legality question worth checking with the local building department.

sections.h2: Shared systems: roofs, heat, water and power
sections.body:
In a two-to-four unit building, a failed shared system affects every household at once, and fixing it usually requires access to every unit. Shared systems deserve first priority in the scope.

The roof and exterior envelope protect all the units together, and water that gets in at the top often damages ceilings and walls in more than one unit. Gutters, flashing, masonry, siding and porches are part of the same envelope.

Heating is a frequent decision point. Many older small multifamily buildings run on a single boiler or furnace serving all units, which means the owner pays for heat and cannot pass it to tenants without separate systems. Converting to individual heating systems can shift that cost to tenants and give them control of their own comfort, but it is a significant scope with its own permits. Repairing or replacing a central boiler can be the right answer in some buildings. We price both paths when the decision matters.

Electrical services and metering raise similar questions. Separate meters for each unit allow tenants to pay their own electric bills. A building with a single service or an outdated panel may need a service upgrade and meter separation, which involves coordination with the utility.

Water supply and the sewer lateral are almost always shared. Old galvanized supply lines reduce water pressure for every unit, and a failing sewer lateral can back up into the lowest unit. A camera inspection of the main line is a sensible step on older buildings.

Our scopes list each shared system with its condition, the recommended action and its cost, separate from the unit-level work.

Many small multifamily buildings are purchased with tenants in place. Renovating around them takes planning, because those tenants still need heat, water, power, safe access and a reasonable degree of quiet while work happens around them.

The usual approach is to phase the project. Vacant units are renovated first, both because the work is faster without a household in place and because a renovated, rent-ready unit starts producing rent at the new level sooner. Occupied units are scheduled as leases turn over or as tenants agree to temporary arrangements, depending on your plan for the building and the local rules that apply.

Building-wide work needs its own sequencing. Replacing a roof or tuckpointing masonry can happen with tenants in place. Replacing a shared boiler or upgrading the electrical service means planned shutdowns with advance notice to every household. Work in shared stairs and hallways has to keep a safe path of travel open at all times. Debris removal and material storage have to be organized so they do not block entries, parking or egress.

Your designated field manager plans the phasing with you before work begins, coordinates the notices your property manager or you need to give, and keeps the occupied units' needs in mind throughout. We document the condition of occupied units before work near them begins, which helps resolve any questions about damage later.

If you prefer to deliver a vacant building, the same phasing logic applies to the order of work, and the scope can be written for a single continuous project instead.

sections.h2: Unit separation, egress and life safety
sections.body:
Codes treat a building with more than one dwelling unit differently from a single-family house, mainly because a fire or other emergency in one unit can endanger the others. Renovations to small multifamily buildings often bring these requirements into play, and some buildings have gone decades without meeting them.

Common items include:

- Fire separation between units, typically rated wall and floor-ceiling assemblies, and attention to penetrations where pipes, ducts and wiring pass between units.
- Smoke and carbon monoxide detection in each unit and, in some buildings, in shared areas.
- Two means of egress where required, which in older stacked buildings often means rear stairs and porches that must be structurally sound.
- Sleeping room egress windows of adequate size, a frequent issue for basement and attic units.
- Handrails and guards on every stair, porch and landing.
- Proper exterior lighting at entries and stairs.

Rear porches and exterior stairs on older stacked buildings deserve particular attention. They carry significant loads, are exposed to weather, and can deteriorate in ways that are not obvious from below. Many cities have specific requirements for them, and their condition should be assessed before you commit to a purchase price.

Our team coordinates permits and inspections with the local building department, verifies that the contractors on the project carry appropriate insurance and licensing, and collects lien waivers. If a building has open code violations, we can scope the corrections as part of the renovation, and Genstone Field Services offers code compliance work for buildings that need ongoing attention.

sections.h2: Scoping for rents, resale and the right strategy
sections.body:
The value of a small multifamily building depends on who will own it next and how they will measure it. An investor underwriting a hold looks at rents and operating costs. An owner-occupant using FHA financing looks at the unit they will live in and the income from the others. A refinance appraisal may consider both comparable sales and the income the building produces. The scope should reflect which of these matters most for your plan.

For a hold or a BRRRR plan, the priority is rental-grade durability, separate utilities where practical, and unit finishes that match the rent level the market supports. Spending more on a unit than its rent can justify ties up capital without improving the return. Using the same materials across all units keeps future maintenance simple.

For a flip, the buyer pool matters. Owner-occupants using FHA financing are a large share of buyers for two-to-four unit buildings in many markets, and they often care most about the owner's unit. A scope that gives the owner's unit a somewhat higher finish level while keeping the rental units durable can widen the appeal. Investors buying a renovated building will look closely at the rent roll and the condition of the systems.

When it helps the decision, we develop multiple ARV plans showing different finish levels and their costs. Conversions within the one-to-four unit range, such as adding a unit to a building, are a bigger step involving zoning, code and permits, and for owner-occupants may fit a Standard FHA 203(k). We scope those carefully and flag the approvals they require.

sections.h2: How Genstone runs a small multifamily project
sections.body:
Every Genstone project follows the same core process, adjusted for the building in front of us.

It starts with a complimentary Pre-Offer Rehab Review. Send the address, the listing, photos and the rent roll if you have one, and we will estimate the anticipated renovation costs, help refine the after-repair value, and tell you whether the numbers support the offer you are considering. For small multifamily buildings we pay particular attention to the shared systems, unit legality and any life-safety items that could change the budget.

After purchase, you receive a detailed scope document and estimate with anticipated labor and materials, building-wide and unit-level work broken out, debris removal included and a draw schedule attached. A designated field manager is assigned for the full project and serves as your primary contact.

Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed and insured local contractors from a national network of thousands. Permits, inspections, lien waivers and contractor compliance are handled as part of the project. You can follow progress, documentation and milestones without being on site.

No upfront payment is required. Draws are tied to completed work, and final payment follows completion and your approval. Completed work carries a one-year workmanship warranty, which does not cover tenant damage or normal wear.

Through the Genstone Companies, you can also access DSCR rental loans and fix-and-flip financing from Genstone Financial, portfolio and rental coverage from Genstone Insurance, and leasing and management from Genstone Property Management. Call (312) 429-2637 to discuss your building.

faqs.q: What types of small multifamily buildings do you renovate?
faqs.a: We renovate two-to-four unit residential buildings of all common types, including side-by-side and up-down duplexes, two-flats and three-flats, triple-deckers, shotgun doubles, fourplexes and older single-family homes that have been converted into units. Each type has its own typical issues, such as rear porches on stacked buildings or shared party walls on side-by-side duplexes, and our scopes reflect the building's configuration.

faqs.q: Can you renovate while tenants are living in some units?
faqs.a: Yes. We phase the work so vacant units are renovated first and building-wide work like roofing or masonry proceeds with tenants in place. Shutdowns of shared systems are scheduled with advance notice, shared stairs and halls stay safe and passable, and the condition of occupied units is documented before nearby work begins. Your field manager plans the phasing with you before the project starts.

faqs.q: Should I separate the utilities in my building?
faqs.a: It depends on the building, the local market and your plans. Separate heating systems and electric meters let tenants pay their own bills and control their own comfort, which can improve your operating income, but the conversion is a significant scope with permits and utility coordination. Sometimes repairing a central boiler is the better choice. We price both paths so you can compare them against the rents and hold period.

faqs.q: How do I know all the units in a building are legal?
faqs.a: The local building and zoning departments are the authority, so check their records before you underwrite on the unit count. Warning signs include basement or attic units with low ceilings, small windows, no second exit or separate meters added informally. During a Pre-Offer Rehab Review, we flag configurations that suggest a legality question so you can confirm the status and price the risk before making an offer.

faqs.q: Can an owner-occupant use FHA 203(k) financing on a fourplex?
faqs.a: Yes. FHA 203(k) loans may be used for eligible two-to-four unit properties, provided the buyer occupies one of the units. Genstone is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor and can scope and bid the renovation for the lender. Structural work, conversions within the one-to-four unit range, or projects above the Limited program cap generally call for a Standard 203(k), which requires an FHA-approved consultant.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix the rear porches on an older stacked building?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Rear porches and exterior stairs on two-flats, three-flats and triple-deckers carry heavy loads, are exposed to weather and are commonly part of the required second means of egress. Deterioration is not always visible from below. We assess their structure, connections and guards during scoping, and repairs or rebuilds are permitted and inspected through the local building department, with the documentation kept in your project file.

faqs.q: How are payments structured on a multifamily renovation?
faqs.a: The same way as every Genstone project. No upfront payment is required, construction draws are tied to completed work, and final payment is due after the project is complete and you have approved it. On phased projects, the draw schedule follows the phases so you are paying for finished units and completed building systems. Lien waivers are collected throughout, so the title stays clean for a refinance or sale.
